primitives.name: RULE I — Field and Goal Geometry (Dimensions, Marking, Goal)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The game shall be played upon a rectangular field, 360 feet in length and 160 leet in width. The lines at the ends of the field shall be termed End Lines. Those at the sides "shall be termed bide Lines and shall extend indefinitely bevond their points of intersection with the goal lines. The Goal Lines shall be established in the field of play ten yards from and parallel to the end lines.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: L = field length [ft]; W = field width [ft]; d_goal = goal-line offset from each end line [yd]; Delta_mark = white-line marking interval [yd]; w_post = goal-post spacing (18 ft 6 in = 18.5 ft) [ft]; h_bar = cross-bar height above ground [ft]. All quantities are lengths (1 yd = 3 ft); posts must exceed 20 ft in height (Sec. 3). Dimensionally homogeneous length set.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE I Sec. 1-3 (PDF p.363, printed Page 7): rectangular field; goal lines parallel to end lines and 10 yd inside them; field of play bounded by goal lines and side lines; end zones between goal lines and end lines; lines marked white at 5-yd intervals; goal posts at middle of each goal line, >20 ft high, 18 ft 6 in apart, cross-bar 10 ft from ground. Source-defect note: OCR renders width as '160 leet' and 'bide Lines'/'bevond' for 'Side Lines'/'beyond'; numbers 360/160/10/5/18.5/10 are legible and taken as printed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Geometric constraint only; holds for the regulation rectangular field. Fails/does not apply for non-regulation or shortened fields agreed under RULE IV, for unmarked fields (Referee must verify marking pre-game, Sec. 2 NOTE), and the goal-post height is a strict lower bound (>20 ft) not an equality. OCR 'leet'/'bide'/'bevond' are transcription artifacts, not physical quantities.
primitives.source_note: OCR artifacts preserved verbatim in quote ('160 leet in width', 'bide Lines', 'bevond'). Primary historical source: Spalding's Official Foot Ball Guide / NCAA Official Rules 1922, ed. Walter Camp; Internet Archive scan (officialnational07nation). No retraction notice (p.1 library mark 'GV', p.2 copyright deposit).

layer2.mapping: Binds the 22-player football state vector to a bounded spatial domain: each player position x_i in [0,L] x [0,W] with end-zone and goal-line boundary conditions; the 5-yd grid discretizes field-position state, and the goal geometry (w_post, h_bar) defines the scoring aperture for kick trajectories. This is the spatial constraint layer of the Coach-Mind dynamical system, not a football 'origin' for any math.
layer2.telemetry: Player/ball tracking coordinates (x,y) calibrated to the 360 ft x 160 ft frame; goal-line and end-zone boundary events; kick cross-bar clearance height. LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE for pre-1922 tracking (no telemetry exists for the era); calibrates only on modern tracking replayed under the 1922 geometry.

primitives.name: RULE V — Scoring Value Vector
primitives.verbatim_quote: The following shall be the value of plays in scoring: Touchdown 6 points. Successful "try" after touchdown... 1 point. Goal from the field 3 points. Safety by opponents 2 points.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: S = scoring-value map from event type to points [points, dimensionless integer count]; events: touchdown=6, successful try after touchdown=1, goal from the field=3, safety by opponents=2. Forfeited game recorded 1 to 0 (printed '1 to [0] in favor of the offended side'; OCR dropped the 0). All values share the single unit 'points'; homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE V (PDF p.367, printed Page 11): game decided by final score at end of four periods; the four scoring values as listed; forfeit score 1-0. The 'try' is the 1922 Try-for-point (RULE X), replacing the pre-1922 place-kick-only Try-for-goal (Changes for 1922, PDF p.356). Source-defect note: forfeit line OCR 'shall be 1 to in favor' omits the 0; value 1-0 confirmed by standard forfeit convention and flagged, not invented.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Reward definition only; valid for the 1922 code. Does NOT carry to other eras (modern NFL touchdown=6 but try=1 or 2, field goal=3, safety=2; pre-1906 values differ). The forfeit 1-0 is an administrative terminal value, not a played score. OCR-dropped '0' in the forfeit line is a transcription defect, quarantined here.
primitives.source_note: Forfeit line OCR defect ('1 to in favor') quarantined; no primitive built on the dropped glyph. Scoring values 6/1/3/2 legible and verbatim.

layer2.mapping: Defines the terminal reward vector of the Coach-Mind Markov decision process: the policy objective is expected cumulative S over the four periods, with the 6/1/3/2 weights setting the relative value of touchdown, try, field goal and safety. This is the reward kernel from which down-distance risk preferences and try-choice (kick vs run/pass) are derived; it is a source invariant mapped into the sim, not a fabricated heuristic.
layer2.telemetry: Per-game scored-event counts by type (touchdowns, successful tries, field goals, safeties) and final scores; calibrates the reward weights and the empirical value of a try attempt vs a field-goal attempt. No sportsbook odds used.

primitives.name: RULE XIX Sec.1 — Necessary Gain on Downs (10 yards in four downs)
primitives.verbatim_quote: having constantly had the ball in its possession, shall not have advanced the ball 10 yards, it shall go to the opponents on the spot of the fifth down, except as provided in Section 2.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: g_i = net yards advanced on consecutive down i [yd]; sum over four downs compared to the 10 yd required gain [yd]; PossessionConstant = predicate that the team 'constantly had the ball in its possession' (broken by opponent possession/recovery or a kick giving a fair equal chance, Sec.2(a)-(b)); Turnover = ball to opponents at the spot of the fifth down. Yards are length; predicates are dimensionless truth values. Formalization of printed prose rule (RULE XIX Sec.1-2), no source equation printed.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE XIX Sec.1 (PDF p.392, printed Page 36): four consecutive downs, constant possession, must advance 10 yd or ball goes to opponents at spot of fifth down. Sec.2 breaks continuity on opponent possession/recovery or a kick crossing the scrimmage line / touched by an opponent; NOTE: an on-side 4th-down kick crossing the line and recovered by offense gives a first down. Sec.3: forward point of ball when dead is the measuring point; Referee shall not rotate the ball. Marginal header '10 yards in 4 downs' interleaves into the OCR body ('a 4 downs. m team'); the quoted span avoids that noise.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Possession-transition invariant for the 1922 code only. Fails when continuity is broken (Sec.2): a kick or change of possession resets the down count, so the naive 'sum of four gains' model is invalid across a punt/kickoff. The 10-yd/4-down constants are era-specific (modern NFL is also 10 yd/4 downs but 1922 field/forward-pass rules differ). Measurement uses the forward point, not the ball center; rotating the ball before measuring is prohibited.
primitives.source_note: OCR marginal-header interleaving ('a 4 downs. m team') quarantined; quote sliced from the clean contiguous span. Predicate-logic LaTeX is an explicit formalization of the printed prose rule, not a printed equation.

layer2.mapping: The core possession-transition (turnover) kernel of the 22-player dynamical system: state = (down d in {1..4}, distance-to-gain y, field position x); the hazard of turnover fires when cumulative gain over the series fails 10 yd under constant possession. This bounds every offensive policy's risk budget and is the constraint that makes 4th-down decisions a stopping problem; mapped as a transition kernel, not an origin myth.
layer2.telemetry: Down-and-distance logs, yards-gained per down, 4th-down conversion and turnover-on-downs rates, punt/kick continuity-breaking events. Calibrates the turnover hazard and the first-down renewal process. No odds inputs.

primitives.name: RULE XVII — Forward Pass Legality, Count, and Receiver Eligibility
primitives.verbatim_quote: The pass must be made from a point at least 5 yards back of the scrimmage line.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: d_pass = distance of the pass origin behind the line of scrimmage [yd] (must be >= 5 yd, Sec.3(a)); N_fp = number of forward passes in one scrimmage [dimensionless count] (only one, Sec.3(b), PDF p.389); EligibleReceiver = predicate that the first toucher of the passer's side was at the snap an end of the line OR >= 1 yd behind the line (Sec.7(a), PDF p.389). Yards are length; count and predicates dimensionless. Formalization of printed prose rule (RULE XVII Sec.3,7); no source equation printed.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE XVII Sec.3(a) (PDF p.388, printed Page 32): pass must be made from >= 5 yd back of the scrimmage line; Sec.3(b) (p.389): only one forward pass per scrimmage; Sec.7(a) (p.389): eligible receivers are ends of the line or players >= 1 yd behind the line at the snap; a player more than one foot but less than one yard back is ineligible in any event. Sec.2: the side not putting the ball in play may not pass forward. Sec.4: a pass striking the ground is incomplete. Pre-4th-down penalties replay the down; on 4th down the ball goes to opponents.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Action-legality invariant for the 1922 code. Fails/changes for later eras (modern pass has no 5-yd depth minimum and different eligibility). The single-pass constraint means a second forward pass in the same scrimmage is illegal (penalty as Sec.3(a)); an ineligible toucher voids completion. The 5-yd depth is a hard geometric gate on the pass action; behind-the-goal-line exceptions (RULE VI Sec.13 NOTE) modify dead-ball handling.
primitives.source_note: Predicate-logic LaTeX explicitly labeled formalization of printed prose (RULE XVII), no printed equation. Quote anchors Sec.3(a) on p.388; count and eligibility clauses cited to p.389.

layer2.mapping: Binds the offensive action mask and the receiver-eligibility information graph: the legal forward-pass action set is gated by pass-origin depth (>=5 yd), a per-scrimmage pass counter (N_fp=1), and an eligibility predicate over the snap-time formation. This is an information-channel / action-constraint isomorphism into the Coach-Mind sim's legal-action generator and deception model (motion/shift must preserve eligibility).
layer2.telemetry: Pass-origin depth behind scrimmage, forward-pass count per play, snap-time receiver eligibility sets, completion/incompletion and ineligible-touch events. Calibrates the action mask and the eligibility graph. LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE for the 1922 era itself (no tracking); calibrates on modern replay under 1922 legality.

primitives.name: RULE X — Try-for-Point After Touchdown
primitives.verbatim_quote: A team which has made a touchdown may add one additional point to its score by putting the ball in play by a scrimmage from any point on or outside the five-yard line, and by successfully executing in a single play any one of the following
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: x = distance of the try scrimmage spot from the goal line [yd] (any point on or outside the five-yard line); S_try = try scoring value [points] = 1; 'single play' = exactly one scrimmage play. The try may score by drop/place-kick goal, by carrying across the goal line (rush or forward pass), or by completing a forward pass in the end zone (Sec.(a)-(c)). Yards length; points dimensionless. Formalization of printed prose rule (RULE X); no source equation printed.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE X (PDF p.378, printed Page 22): after a touchdown the scoring side may add 1 point by a single scrimmage play from on/outside the 5-yd line, via kick, run, or forward pass. Offensive foul or illegal/incomplete forward pass forfeits the point; defensive foul awards the point without further play (whether or not the try succeeded); fouls on both sides replay the try. Whether successful or not, ball then put in play by kick-off. This is the 1922 innovation replacing the place-kick-only Try-for-goal (Changes for 1922, PDF p.356).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Post-touchdown sub-process invariant for the 1922 code only. The foul-award asymmetry is critical: a defensive foul gives the point even if the try failed, so 'try success probability' alone is an incomplete model. Modern codes allow a 2-point conversion from a different spot and differ; the 1922 try is strictly 1 point. The single-play constraint forbids a second attempt absent a both-sides foul replay.
primitives.source_note: Predicate-logic LaTeX explicitly labeled formalization of printed prose (RULE X), no printed equation. 1922 Try-for-point innovation corroborated by 'Changes in the Rules for 1922' (PDF p.356).

layer2.mapping: A post-touchdown single-play sub-MDP with a 1-point terminal reward and an asymmetric foul-award branch: the offense chooses kick/run/pass from a selectable spot x>=5 yd, and the defense's foul decision can award the point regardless of play outcome. This nests inside the scoring kernel (p2) and creates a game-theoretic spot-selection and foul-deterrence problem in the Coach-Mind sim.
layer2.telemetry: Try spot distance, try mode (kick/run/pass), try success, defensive-foul-awarded points, both-sides-foul replays. Calibrates the try sub-policy and the foul-award branch. No odds inputs.

primitives.name: RULE VI Sec.16 — Safety by Defending-Side Impetus
primitives.verbatim_quote: ball in possession of a player guarding his own goal is declared dead by the Referee, any part of it being on, above or behind the goal line, provided the impetus which caused it to pass from outside the goal line to or behind the goal line was given by the side defending the goal.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: DeadOnBehindOwnGoal = predicate that the ball in possession of a player guarding his own goal is declared dead with any part on/above/behind that goal line; Impetus_defense = predicate that the impetus carrying the ball from outside to/behind the goal line was given by the side defending the goal (from own kick/pass/snap/fumble, Sec.16(a), or a kick rebounding off an opponent/own player behind the line, Sec.16(b)). Safety awards 2 points to the opponents (RULE V, p2). Predicates dimensionless truth values. Formalization of printed prose rule (RULE VI Sec.16); no source equation printed.
primitives.assumptions: Printed RULE VI Sec.16 (PDF p.373, printed Page 17): a Safety requires BOTH a dead ball on/behind the defender's own goal line AND that the impetus was supplied by the defending side. Also a safety on an incomplete forward pass behind one's own goal line, or a foul whose penalty leaves the ball behind one's own goal line, or a kick from behind the goal line crossing the extended side line before being touched. Contrast Touchback (Sec.15): impetus given by an OPPONENT yields a touchback, not a safety. OCR stray period 'when the . ball' avoided in the quoted span.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Causality-gated terminal-event invariant. The defining failure mode is mis-attributing impetus: if the opponent supplied the impetus the event is a touchback (no score), not a safety (2 pts). Thus a model that scores 'ball dead behind goal line = safety' is WRONG without the impetus predicate. Era-specific to the 1922 code; the impetus causality test is the sovereign invariant, not the mere dead-ball spot.
primitives.source_note: OCR stray period ('when the . ball') quarantined; quote sliced from clean span. Predicate-logic LaTeX explicitly labeled formalization of printed prose (RULE VI Sec.16), no printed equation.

layer2.mapping: Binds a causality (impetus-attribution) state variable to the terminal-event classifier of the 22-player system: the same dead-ball geometry maps to safety (2 pts to opponent) vs touchback (no score) purely by which side supplied the impetus. This is an impetus/causality isomorphism — the football analogue of attributing momentum transfer to a source — and vetoes any spot-only scoring classifier in the Coach-Mind sim.
layer2.telemetry: Dead-ball spot relative to goal line, ball-carrier impetus source (which side last kicked/passed/snapped/fumbled), safety vs touchback rulings. Calibrates the impetus-attribution classifier. LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE for the 1922 era; calibrates on modern ruling logs.

reasoning_traces.think: Reading the 1922 Official Foot Ball Rules as a constrained dynamical system rather than a nostalgia artifact reveals a complete, self-consistent specification of the 22-player game: a bounded spatial domain (p1, RULE I, PDF p.363), a terminal reward vector (p2, RULE V, p.367), a possession-transition hazard (p3, RULE XIX, p.392), an action-legality and information channel (p4, RULE XVII, p.388-389), a post-score sub-process (p5, RULE X, p.378), and a causality-gated terminal classifier (p6, RULE VI Sec.16, p.373). The first discipline is to keep Layer 1 sovereign: every number here is printed, not invented. The field is 360 ft by 160 ft, goal lines ten yards inside the end lines, posts 18 ft 6 in apart with a 10 ft cross-bar; scoring is touchdown 6, try 1, field goal 3, safety 2; a team must advance 10 yards in four consecutive downs under constant possession or surrender the ball at the spot of the fifth down. These are the source invariants. The second discipline is to refuse fabricated origins: nothing in this football code is a 'football origin' for a pure theorem, and nothing here licenses a toy heuristic like success equals force over fatigue. The reward vector is a definition, the downs rule is a transition kernel, the pass rule is an action mask, and the safety rule is a causality test. When I map them into the Coach-Mind sim I am building explicit [ISOMORPHISM] and [DERIVED KERNEL] bridges, not claiming the 1922 committee derived modern control theory. The deepest invariant is the impetus test in p6: a ball dead behind the goal line is a safety only if the defending side supplied the impetus; if the opponent supplied it, the event is a touchback and scores nothing. A spot-only classifier would systematically mis-score these events, so the causality predicate is the sovereign feature, exactly as momentum attribution is sovereign in a collision analysis. The downs kernel p3 is the risk budget: because continuity is broken by a kick or a change of possession (Sec.2), the naive 'sum four gains' model is invalid across a punt, and the on-side-kick recovery NOTE shows the committee already understood that a kick crossing the line resets the hazard. The forward-pass rule p4 is a geometric and combinatorial gate: the pass must originate at least five yards behind the line, only one forward pass is legal per scrimmage, and the first eligible toucher must have been an end or a man at least one yard back at the snap. That last clause creates a sharp eligibility boundary — a player more than one foot but less than one yard back is ineligible in any event — which is precisely the kind of discrete constraint that an action-mask generator must encode rather than smooth away. The try-for-point p5 is the era's signature innovation: the 1922 Changes (p.356) replaced the place-kick-only try-for-goal with a single scrimmage play from on or outside the five-yard line that may score by kick, run, or pass, and the foul-award asymmetry (defensive foul awards the point even if the try failed) means a model of try success probability alone is incomplete. Reading these together, the code is a layered constraint stack: geometry bounds state, reward defines objective, the downs hazard defines turnover risk, the pass rule defines the legal action set and the deception surface, the try defines a nested sub-game, and impetus defines terminal causality. The honest core-read focused on the official rules code (PDF pp. 355-424); the surrounding season reviews, rosters, and records were scanned at text level and contain no additional sovereign rule invariants, and the OCR defects (160 'leet', 'bide Lines', the dropped forfeit zero, the marginal-header interleaving on p.392) are quarantined in source notes rather than built upon. This is how a polymath audits a rules book: extract the invariant stack, label every formalization as a formalization of prose, preserve the printed defects verbatim, and map each layer into the sim with calibrated telemetry or an honest LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE for the pre-telemetry era.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The hidden state of this code is the scar of the old mass-momentum game. The Rules Committee report (PDF p.357) states that the change from 'the old style foot ball to the modern game had been practically completed' and that a 'good all-around open game has at last been fairly established,' with future changes confined to detail. That sentence is the genealogy: the forward pass, the neutral zone, the seven-men-on-the-line requirement, and the 10-yards-in-four-downs hazard were legislated to break the closed, collision-heavy game and open space. The 1922 try-for-point (Changes, p.356) is the latest sediment of that lineage — it widens the scoring surface after a touchdown from a single place-kick to a run-or-pass scrimmage, rewarding the open game the committee had spent years constructing. The Foot Ball Code (p.360-361) is the moral sediment: holding, side-line coaching, and 'beating the ball' are prohibited not merely as fouls but as threats to the game's integrity, showing the committee legislating against the incentive to 'beat the rules.' Reading the invariants retrocausally, each constraint is a scar tissue over a prior failure mode.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Under pressure the beliefs clash recursively. The coach's comfort call on fourth down is to punt and pin the opponent, because the downs hazard (p3) makes a failed conversion a turnover at the spot — but the defensive coordinator's tendency trap is to stack the line expecting the punt-safe run, which the offense can exploit with a legal forward pass only if the pass-origin depth (>=5 yd, p4) and the single eligible receiver are satisfied. The quarterback's internal clock must resolve the snap-count and the five-yard depth before the ball is put in play, while the defense reads the same formation to infer eligibility. Each agent models the others: the coach models the DC's punt expectation, the DC models the coach's risk budget under the 10-yd hazard, and the QB models the defense's read of the eligibility graph. The try-for-point (p5) sharpens this: the offense must believe the defense will not foul (because a defensive foul awards the point regardless), while the defense must believe the offense cannot simply run it in, creating a recursive deterrence game on a single play from a selectable spot.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Physics and psychology veto several high-EV simplifications. The impetus rule (p6) vetoes any call that treats 'ball dead behind the goal line' as an automatic safety: if the opponent supplied the impetus it is a touchback worth zero, so a two-point expectation built on spot alone is physically wrong about momentum attribution. The eligibility boundary (p4) vetoes a high-EV pass to a lineman who is more than one foot but less than one yard back — he is ineligible in any event, so the pass is void and the down is lost, a legal veto over the apparent open receiver. The foul-award asymmetry (p5) vetoes a deliberate-foul-on-the-try strategy: a defensive foul hands the offense the point even if the try failed, so the 'smart' foul is dominated. And the downs continuity rule (p3, Sec.2) vetoes summing gains across a punt, because the kick resets the hazard. These are cross-layer vetoes where the rule's causality and geometry override a naive expected-value call.

reasoning_traces.think: The second trace audits the measurement and enforcement layer that makes the invariant stack operational, because a rule that cannot be measured or enforced is not a sovereign invariant in practice. RULE XIX Sec.3 (PDF p.393) fixes the forward point of the ball when dead as the determining point in measuring and forbids the Referee from rotating the ball before measuring — this is a measurement convention that removes an ambiguity which would otherwise let the same physical spot yield different down-and-distance states. RULE XXVII (p.404-405) makes the Linesman mark distance with two rods connected by a chain ten yards in length, the physical embodiment of the 10-yd gain constant in p3; the chain is the calibration artifact of the turnover hazard. The penalty summary (p.407-408) is a graded cost schedule: two yards for a fourth time-out request, five for off-side and illegal formation, ten for throwing a forward pass to ground before fourth down, fifteen for holding by the offense and for pass interference, twenty-five for not being ready at the second half, and half the distance to the goal for an illegal return or a striking foul. Reading this schedule as a cost kernel, the committee priced infractions by how much they corrupt the invariant stack: formation and off-side fouls distort the spatial and eligibility constraints (p1, p4) and cost five to fifteen yards; conduct fouls that endanger players (striking, roughing the kicker, p.393 RULE XXI) carry disqualification plus half-distance, the maximum non-forfeit cost. The enforcement jurisdiction is itself partitioned: the Referee is sole judge of the ball's position and progress (RULE XXV Sec.6, p.398), the Umpire judges player conduct and position (RULE XXVI, p.402), the Linesman marks distance and reports off-side and neutral-zone encroachment (RULE XXVII, p.404-405), and the Field Judge keeps time with a stop-watch started when the ball is actually put in play, not when the Referee orders play (RULE XXVIII, p.406). That last clause is a subtle bioenergetic and clock invariant: the 60-minute game (RULE IV, p.365-366) is four 15-minute periods of actual play, exclusive of time taken out, so the duty cycle is defined by ball-in-play time, not wall-clock time. The darkness clause (RULE IV Sec.2) lets the Referee shorten the four periods to equal lengths before play, an early recognition that the temporal boundary condition can be renegotiated to preserve the four-equal-period structure. Putting measurement, cost, jurisdiction, and clock together, the enforcement layer is what turns the printed invariants into a well-posed dynamical system: the chain calibrates distance, the forward-point convention calibrates the state, the penalty schedule prices constraint violations, the jurisdiction partition assigns observables to observers, and the stop-watch defines the time base. For the Coach-Mind sim this means the telemetry channel is not optional decoration — down-and-distance, the forward-point spot, foul type and yardage, and ball-in-play clock are the observables that calibrate the kernels p2-p6. Where the 1922 era has no such telemetry, I label it LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE rather than fabricate tracking, and I calibrate the structure on modern replay under the 1922 geometry and legality. The honest refusal to invent era telemetry is itself a sovereign discipline: the invariant stack is fully extractable from the printed code, but its empirical calibration is era-bound, and saying so plainly is the difference between a sovereign extraction and a laundered one.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The enforcement layer carries its own genealogy. The Report (p.357-359) laments that competent officials 'hesitate to inflict penalties, lest they thereby incur the dissatisfaction or hostility of the authorities of the college involved,' and appeals to colleges to back fearless officials. That is the scar: a rule code without institutional backing decays into selective enforcement, so the committee codified jurisdiction (Referee/Umpire/Linesman/Field Judge) and a graded penalty schedule to make enforcement legible and defensible. The 1922 Changes (p.356) note that 'Approved Rulings, as far as possible, have been incorporated into the Rules' and that the shift rule was made 'more clear and more simple of enforcement' — sediment of years of disputed rulings hardened into printed text. The chain and the forward-point convention are the material scars of measurement disputes, frozen into RULE XXVII and RULE XIX Sec.3 so that the same spot cannot be argued into two different states.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The enforcement game is recursive theory of mind among officials and captains. The Referee must model whether a captain's time-out request is genuine injury or a delay tactic, because the fourth request costs two yards (penalty summary, p.407) — a priced signal that changes the captain's incentive. The Umpire, positioned behind the defending side (RULE XXVI Sec.1), models holding by reading the offense's intent, while the offense models the Umpire's sightline to hide holding. The Linesman models off-side and neutral-zone encroachment from the side, and the defense models the Linesman's angle to time a jump. The Field Judge's stop-watch, started on actual ball-in-play, is a shared clock each agent models to manage the two-minute and end-of-half boundaries. The captain's appeal is restricted to the captain (the Code, p.361: 'let your captain do the talking'), a protocol that reduces noisy multi-agent signaling to a single channel the Referee can adjudicate.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Measurement and clock physics veto naive calls. The forward-point convention (RULE XIX Sec.3) vetoes any down-and-distance computation that uses the ball center or a rotated ball, because the printed determining point is the forward point when dead — using the wrong reference shifts the state and can manufacture a false first down. The stop-watch invariant (RULE XXVIII) vetoes wall-clock game models: because time is exclusive of time taken out and starts on actual ball-in-play, a model that runs the clock during a dead ball overstates the remaining duty cycle and mis-prices end-of-half decisions. The penalty schedule vetoes the 'take the foul' calculus on conduct fouls: roughing the kicker is fifteen yards plus disqualification (RULE XXI Sec.2, p.393), so a high-EV hit on the kicker is dominated by the ejection cost. And the darkness clause vetoes assuming fixed 15-minute periods when the Referee has lawfully shortened them — the temporal boundary condition is part of the state, not a constant.

universal_lens: A polymath reads this 1922 rules code as a layered constraint stack on a 22-agent dynamical system: geometry bounds the state space (p1), a reward vector defines the objective (p2), a downs hazard defines turnover risk (p3), an action mask and eligibility graph define the legal action set and deception surface (p4), a nested single-play sub-game defines post-score choice (p5), and an impetus-causality predicate defines terminal classification (p6). The audit lens is invariant-first: extract printed constants verbatim, label every predicate-logic expression as a formalization of prose, quarantine OCR defects, and refuse fabricated origins or toy heuristics.
gsi_mapping: For GSI the code maps to the collision and bioenergetics interface: the neutral zone and line of scrimmage (RULE VI Sec.3, p.368) are a shear interface between two eleven-body packs, and the impetus predicate (p6) is the football analogue of attributing momentum transfer to a source — the same causality question that governs axonal shear in a collision. The 60-minute four-period structure with a stop-watch on actual ball-in-play (RULE IV, p.365; RULE XXVIII, p.406) is a bioenergetic duty cycle, and the graded conduct-foul schedule (RULE XXI, p.393) is a clinical-telemetry proxy for injury-mechanism severity. This is a mapping lens, not a claim that the 1922 book contains biomechanics; era telemetry is LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE.
gse_mapping: For GSE the invariants compile into the Coach-Mind sim: p2 is the reward kernel, p3 the possession-transition (turnover) hazard, p4 the legal-action mask and deception/eligibility graph, p5 a nested try sub-MDP with a foul-award branch, and p6 a causality-gated terminal classifier. The downs hazard and the foul-award asymmetry structure tail risk in a DFS/portfolio sense — concentrated turnover exposure and dominated deliberate-foul strategies — without any sportsbook odds.
